title: Arena and agent swarms
description: Several runs or agents at once: compare them for the best answer, split up a big task, and use the same trick to measure quality.

steps.question: A model answered once. How do you know that is its best answer and not just the first one it came up with?
steps.answer: You don't, because there is nothing to compare it with. That is why people run several attempts: a single answer can be weak, and without a second one beside it you won't notice. Both tricks in this lesson, the arena and the swarm, are built on this idea.

steps.text: When one model run is not enough, you start several at once. Two common tricks are the arena and the swarm. The first one also has a bonus that every agent builder will use.

steps.imagePrompt: Three small friendly robots stand side by side, each holding up its own different drawing of the same apple, while a large magnifying glass hovers above them comparing the drawings.
steps.caption: Several answers to one request, so you have something to choose from

steps.text: Arena mode: several models (or several runs of one model) answer the same request. Then you compare the answers and pick the best one.
Why: a single answer can be weak and you won't notice, because there is nothing to compare it with. The arena gives you a choice and shows honestly which model handles your task better.

A person is not the only one who can compare. You can use a judge model: you give it the answers and the criteria (“rate accuracy, completeness, brevity”) and it picks the winner. A judge is cheaper than your time and never gets tired.

steps.definition: A separate model that gets several answers and the grading criteria, and names the best one. It judges by the standards you set: accuracy, completeness, brevity.
steps.example: Three drafts of a letter + the criterion “polite and under 6 sentences” → the judge picks the second and explains why.

steps.text: Now the bonus: this same trick is the basis of agent quality checks. Prepare a set of typical tasks, run the agent through them after every change, and judge the answers (yourself or with a judge model). That is how builders find out whether things got better or worse. Without it, every “improvement” is guesswork.
The second trick is the agent swarm. Several agents work together: an orchestrator splits the task into pieces, hands them to worker agents, and then collects the results into one answer.

A swarm example: “study 20 reviews and write a summary.” The orchestrator gives five reviews each to four workers, they work in parallel, and then the results are merged. It is faster, and each worker keeps only a small piece in its context instead of everything at once.

steps.caption: Two tabs: arena and swarm. The answers, the judge's scores and the workers' speed are just an example

steps.instruction: Put the swarm's work in order:
items: The workers run in parallel, each on its own piece
The orchestrator splits the task into parts
The orchestrator merges their results into one answer
The orchestrator hands the pieces to the workers
steps.explain: The orchestrator first splits the task and hands out the pieces, the workers run at the same time, and only then are their results merged.

steps.text: The price: both the arena and the swarm mean many requests, which means many tokens. You use them when quality or speed matters more than cost.

A common misconception: “more agents is always better.” It is not. Coordination eats tokens on its own and adds its own mistakes. For a simple task a swarm is overkill: one good agent will do better than five unneeded ones.

pairs.def: one question, several answers: pick the best
one big task, split between workers
a simple task where coordination only gets in the way

steps.situation: You need to quickly digest 40 long reviews and write one overall summary.
options: A swarm: hand the pieces to workers and merge the results
One agent reading everything in a single window
An arena of three models on the whole batch at once
steps.explain: The task splits into independent pieces. That is the swarm's profile. An arena costs more here with no gain in quality.

steps.text: Practice. After the lesson, set up an arena of two Meta models. Ask a question in a normal chat. By default Muse Spark 1.3 answers. Then go to Settings → Model, choose Muse Wonder 1.0, open a new chat and ask the same question. You are the judge: which answer is more accurate, which is shorter, which is more honest? Notice the price too: Muse Wonder costs several times more than Spark. Then switch back to Auto, where Muse Spark 1.3 comes first. Muse Glimmer has open weights, so you can't pick it in the app, but you can run it somewhere else and put it into an arena in just the same way.

In short. The arena means several answers to one request, and you pick the best; a judge model can do the judging, and the same trick is the basic way to measure an agent's quality. The swarm means an orchestrator splits a task between workers and collects the result. Both are powerful and both are expensive, so use them when quality matters more than cost.

options: Several answers to one request, and you pick the best
A queue of requests to one model, in turn
Two chats arguing with each other until one wins
questions.explain: The arena compares several answers and picks the best.

options: A model that compares answers against criteria
A person who rewrites the answers by hand
A model that makes answers generate faster
questions.explain: The judge gets the answers and the criteria, then picks the best one. This is also how agent quality is measured.

questions.q: What does an agent swarm do?
options: Splits a task between several agents and collects the result
Makes one model answer several times in a row
Simply slows down the answer to make it more reliable
questions.explain: The orchestrator hands out subtasks to workers and collects the result.

questions.q: When is a swarm a bad idea?
options: For a simple task: coordination costs more than it helps
Never: a swarm is always faster than one agent
Only when the task doesn't fit in one window
questions.explain: Coordination eats tokens on its own. On a simple task, one agent does better.
